title: Closing down the project's finances
blurb: Close a project's finances properly: settle what's owed, stop further charges, reconcile, release what's left, hand over to BAU and learn.
question: A leisure centre has been handed over to the council's facilities team. Some supplier invoices are still arriving, £30k of contingency is unspent, and the contractor's retention is held for a twelve-month defects period. What must the project manager do to close the project's finances properly, and why does it matter?

teach.h: Finishing the money, not just the work
teach.body: Financial close-down formally brings the project's finances to an end: every obligation is settled, no further costs can be charged, the final cost is reconciled and reported, unused funds are released, ongoing costs and assets pass to business as usual, and the records are archived. In plain English: pay what you owe, shut the tap, count up, give back what's left, hand over the running costs, file it and learn from it.

steps.label: Close cost codes
steps.sub: No further charges can be booked

steps.label:
Release and
transfer
steps.sub: Unused contingency back; running costs to BAU

teach.caption: The sponsor (or the governance body) signs off the financial closure.

teach.body: Open cost codes let unrelated costs keep landing on the project, distorting its final cost. Unpaid suppliers lead to disputes and damage relationships. An accurate final cost is needed to judge the business case, to inform benefits reviews and to improve future estimates. Releasing unused money lets the organisation fund other work. Clear handover means someone owns the running costs, and archived records satisfy audit and governance.

items.sub: All work accepted by the facilities team

items.sub: Cost codes then closed to new charges

items.sub: Retention released by the agreed owner

teach.caption: A retention is part of each payment held back until defects are fixed. It is recorded as outstanding at closure, with an agreed owner to release it later.

teach.h: What the final financial report covers
head: Item
What it shows
rows: Outturn against the baseline, with reasons
How change requests altered the budget
How much was used, on what, and released
Retentions or disputes, and their owner
Assets and running costs passed to BAU
What to do differently next time

teach.text: Exam trap: unused contingency is not the PM's to spend on extra features, the team or another project. It is released back through governance. And timing matters: settle the final invoices before the cost codes close, or late bills will have nowhere to go.

teach.body: If a project is cancelled part-way, perhaps because the business case no longer stands, its finances still need a full close-down: contracts terminated as their terms allow, cancellation charges and work done paid for, actuals reconciled, remaining funds released and lessons captured. A cancelled project's money matters as much as a finished one's, and possibly more, because the organisation needs to know what it spent without getting the benefits.

rows.label: When
values: Partly per release; finally after the last

rows.label: Running costs
values: Handed over as each release goes live

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Confirm all work is complete and accepted, then settle final invoices, claims and retentions.
Close cost codes so no further charges are booked, and reconcile final actuals against the budget.
Release unused contingency and transfer assets and ongoing costs to BAU.
Produce the final financial report, archive the records and capture financial lessons.
Say WHY for each: control, accurate final cost, compliance, freeing funds, better future estimates.
Close-down settles every obligation and stops further charges.
Reconcile final actuals with the budget and explain variances.
Unused contingency goes back through governance; it is never spent on extras.
Assets and running costs pass to BAU with a named owner.
Final financial report, archived records and lessons, signed off by the sponsor.

summary: You can now describe the steps in closing a project's finances, from confirming acceptance and settling invoices to closing cost codes, reconciling, releasing contingency and handing running costs to BAU. You can also explain why each step matters, including when a project closes early.

A.q: Which of the following is NOT normally part of closing down a project's finances?
options: Settling the final supplier invoices
Closing the project's cost codes
Spending the leftover contingency
Reconciling actuals against budget
A.why: Unused contingency is released back to the organisation through governance, not spent to use it up.

whyNot.0: Paying final invoices is a core close-down step.
whyNot.1: Closing cost codes stops further charges and is a core step.
whyNot.3: Reconciliation establishes the true final cost and is a core step.

A.q: A project finishes with £15k of its contingency unspent. What should happen to it?
options: It is released back to the organisation
It is shared out as a team bonus
It is kept by the PM for future projects
It is spent on extra features for users
A.why: Contingency exists for the project's risks. Once the project ends, any balance is released back to the sponsoring organisation through governance.

whyNot.1: Contingency is for risks, never a reward fund.
whyNot.2: The PM doesn't own contingency; it belongs to the sponsoring organisation.
whyNot.3: Extra features would be new scope needing change control, not a use of leftover contingency.

A.q: Why are final actual costs reconciled against the budget at closure?
options: To work out the team's annual pay rises
To set the next project's contingency
To restart the schedule for a new phase
To confirm the true final cost and why
A.why: Reconciliation confirms the project's true final cost and explains the variances against the baseline, informing the business case review, audit and future estimating.

whyNot.0: Pay reviews are an HR matter, not the purpose of reconciliation.
whyNot.1: Lessons may inform future estimates, but each project sets its own contingency from its own risks.
whyNot.2: Closure ends the project; it doesn't restart its schedule.

B.q: Why should a project's financial records be archived at closure?
options: So the budget can be reopened later
So they're available for audit and reference
So the final invoices can be paid again
So the sponsor can avoid formal sign-off
B.why: Archived records support audit and governance, and let future projects refer back to actual costs and lessons.

whyNot.0: Archiving closes the record; it isn't a way to reopen the budget.
whyNot.2: Archiving helps prevent double payment, not cause it.
whyNot.3: Archiving doesn't replace the sponsor's formal sign-off.

B.q: At closure, one supplier invoice is unpaid because its amount is disputed. What is the recommended approach?
options: Close the accounts and leave it unpaid
Pay the full amount without any checks
Resolve the dispute before final closure
Charge it quietly to another project
B.why: Disputes should be resolved before final closure, or, if that can't happen, formally recorded as an outstanding liability with an agreed owner, so nothing is left hanging.

whyNot.0: Closing with an unresolved dispute leaves a liability with no owner and risks legal action.
whyNot.1: Paying without checking could mean paying for work not done or not to standard.
whyNot.3: Moving costs to another project hides the true final cost and breaks governance.

B.q: Who normally gives the formal authorisation that a project's finances are closed?
options: The project sponsor
The main supplier
The project team
The end users
B.why: The sponsor, accountable for the business case and the investment, signs off the project's closure, including its finances, in line with governance.

whyNot.1: A supplier settles its own contract but doesn't authorise the client's closure.
whyNot.2: The team supports closure activities but has no authority to sign it off.
whyNot.3: Users accept deliverables; they don't authorise financial closure.

C.q: A contractor's 5% retention is held until a twelve-month defects period ends, but the project is closing now. What is the BEST approach?
options: Pay the retention now so the project can close
Record it as outstanding with an agreed owner
Keep the whole project open for twelve months
Cancel the retention because the work is done
C.why: The retention protects the client until defects are fixed. At closure it is recorded as an outstanding item and handed to an agreed owner (for example the facilities team) to release when the period ends.

whyNot.0: Paying early removes the protection the retention is meant to give.
whyNot.2: Keeping the whole project open for a year wastes effort and lets unrelated costs creep in.
whyNot.3: The retention is contractual; it can't simply be cancelled.

C.q: Which THREE should appear in a final financial report? 1: Final cost against budget, with reasons for variances. 2: Contingency used and released. 3: Each team member's performance rating. 4: Outstanding liabilities such as retentions.
options: 1, 2 and 4
1, 2 and 3
2, 3 and 4
1, 3 and 4
C.why: The final financial report covers the outturn and variances, how contingency was used and released, and anything still outstanding, with its owner.

whyNot.1: Performance ratings are an HR matter, not part of the financial report, and this leaves out outstanding liabilities.
whyNot.2: Performance ratings don't belong in it, and this leaves out the final cost against budget.
whyNot.3: Performance ratings don't belong in it, and this leaves out contingency.

C.q: A sponsor cancels a project halfway because its business case no longer stands. What happens to the project's finances?
options: They're simply left open in case it restarts
They're moved straight into the BAU budget
They're closed down formally, as for any project
They're written off without any reconciliation
C.why: A cancelled project still needs a full close-down: terminate contracts as their terms allow, pay what is due, reconcile, release remaining funds and capture lessons.

whyNot.0: Leaving finances open lets costs keep accruing with no control.
whyNot.1: Project costs don't become BAU costs just because the project stopped.
whyNot.3: Reconciliation matters even more when the organisation has spent money without getting the benefits.

reteach.title: Moving out of a rented flat
reteach.question: You're moving out of a rented flat. What would you do with the money side before handing back the keys?

blocks.h: Settle up, switch off, hand over
blocks.body: You check everything is done (cleaned, repaired) and agreed with the landlord. You pay the final bills, then close the utility accounts so no new charges appear in your name. You check what you actually spent against what you planned. Your deposit, held back in case of damage, comes back later once the landlord is satisfied: just like a retention. Ongoing bills pass to the new tenant, like running costs passing to BAU. You keep the paperwork in case of disputes.

blocks.text: Forget to close the energy account and you'll keep getting the next tenant's bills: the same as leaving a project cost code open.

explain.body: Close-down starts by confirming every deliverable is complete and accepted. Only then are final invoices paid, claims settled and retentions recorded, so the organisation pays for what it has actually received.

test.q: Before the final supplier payments are released, what should the project manager confirm?
options: The lessons report is written
The work is complete and accepted
The cost codes are already closed
The contingency has been spent
test.why: Final payments should only be made for work that is complete and accepted against its criteria.

whyNot.0: Lessons can be finished later; they don't govern payment.
whyNot.2: Closing codes before paying final invoices leaves those payments nowhere to be booked.
whyNot.3: Contingency is released, not spent, at closure.

explain.h: Shut the tap and count up
explain.body: Once final costs are in, cost codes are closed so nothing more can be charged to the project. The final actuals are reconciled with the budget and variances explained.

test.q: Three months after handover, staff are still booking time to the old project's cost code. Which close-down step was missed?
options: Releasing contingency
Archiving the records
Transferring the assets
Closing the cost codes
test.why: Closing cost codes stops any further charges landing on the project, keeping its final cost accurate.

whyNot.0: Releasing contingency returns unused funds; it doesn't stop bookings.
whyNot.1: Archiving stores records; it doesn't block new charges.
whyNot.2: Transferring assets passes ownership to BAU; bookings need the codes closed.

explain.body: Unused contingency goes back to the organisation. Assets pass to their BAU owner, and ongoing running costs (licences, maintenance, support) move to the BAU operating budget so someone is accountable for them.

test.q: A new booking system has handed over, but its annual support contract continues. Where should that cost sit from now on?
options: In the project's contingency
In the supplier's own accounts
In the original capital budget
In the BAU operating budget
test.why: Ongoing running costs belong to the business that uses the system, so they transfer to the BAU operating budget at handover.

whyNot.0: Contingency is released at closure and was for project risks.
whyNot.1: The organisation pays for support; it can't move the cost onto the supplier.
whyNot.2: The capital budget funded creating the asset and closes with the project.

explain.body: The final financial report sets out the final cost, variances, contingency use and outstanding items. Records are archived for audit, and financial lessons (such as where estimates were wrong) are captured to improve future projects. The sponsor signs off.

test.q: How do financial lessons captured at closure MOST help the organisation?
options: They raise this project's final budget
They improve future estimates and budgets
They remove the need for future sign-off
They let codes stay open for new work
test.why: Comparing estimates with actual outturns shows where estimating went wrong, so future budgets are more realistic.

whyNot.0: The project is closing; lessons don't change its budget.
whyNot.2: Governance sign-off is still needed on every project.
whyNot.3: Cost codes should be closed; lessons don't change that.
